excerpt: Beside a historic circular water divider, SHO KATAOKA ARCHITECTS creates a house where an engawa-like threshold, flowing water and cherry blossoms connect domestic life with the town.
editorial:
Some of Japan’s most meaningful public places began as works of utility. In Kuji, Kawasaki, the Nikaryō Canal Kuji Cylindrical Divider belongs to this lineage. Built in 1941 to distribute water from the Tama River across surrounding farmland, the circular structure has gradually taken on a new life. Water continues to move through its basin, cherry trees mark the seasons, and residents gather along the promenade. Engineering has become landscape, while landscape has become part of the neighbourhood’s cultural identity.
The residence designed by Sho Kataoka Architects sits within this living civic setting. Its significance lies in the relationship it establishes between a private home and the town's shared life. The canal is present as sound, movement and memory. The promenade carries the familiar rhythm of neighbours passing, pausing and meeting. Architecture becomes a means of bringing these everyday experiences into the home, allowing domestic life to remain connected to the wider community.
This connection begins at the brick-paved earthen-floor room facing the promenade. It is a place of arrival, but also a room for sitting, talking and observing life outside. Wide sliding doors extend its atmosphere towards the garden and the water, creating a contemporary interpretation of the engawa. Within Japanese culture, the engawa has always carried more than a practical role. It gives form to the space between interior and exterior, family and neighbour, shelter and season. In Kuji, this tradition is translated into a generous social threshold suited to contemporary urban life. A neighbour may stop for a brief conversation. A resident may sit near the entrance and watch the cherry trees move in the wind. Friends can gather near the street, while the more personal rooms remain farther within the house. These modest encounters reveal an important civic quality. The residence participates in the town through hospitality, proximity and attention, turning the edge of the home into a place where people can meet naturally.
The architectural composition develops from this social base. A slender spiral staircase connects a series of shifting levels, while timber shelves, steps and platforms give each activity its own position within the larger volume. Working, dining, reading and rest are understood as parts of a continuous domestic landscape. The interior feels closely choreographed, yet its character comes from how people inhabit it across the day.
Windows establishes a sequence of relationships with Kuji. The cylindrical divider appears as a familiar civic form. The cherry canopy brings colour and seasonal movement into the rooms. Wider openings gather the canal, bridge and surrounding streets into the life of the house. Each view has its own scale and tempo, encouraging residents to experience the neighbourhood through a succession of framed moments. This approach gives the house an almost cinematic quality. Water, foliage, architecture and daily movement enter the interior in changing compositions. Spring blossom, summer shade, rainfall, and winter branches create a calendar experienced through the same rooms and thresholds. Time becomes visible through repetition, giving the residents an intimate awareness of the place they inhabit.
Warm timber, pale plaster, brick and built-in furniture support this relationship between architecture and everyday ritual. The materials establish continuity across the levels and provide a calm setting for objects, conversation and changing daylight. Their role is cultural as much as visual, connecting contemporary living with familiar Japanese ideas of tactility, seasonality and spatial transition.
Sho Kataoka Architects presents the detached house as part of a broader urban culture. The project brings people, infrastructure, nature and domestic life into a shared composition, demonstrating how private architecture can contribute to the character of a neighbourhood. Its identity grows from an attentive reading of place: the movement of water, the presence of trees, the habits of residents and the social life of the street. In Kuji, the home becomes both a personal sanctuary and an active participant in the city.

excerpt: For The Prince Park Tower Tokyo’s renewal, Mitsui Designtec Co., Ltd. introduces "THE TOKYO FUSION," a design concept that dissolves the boundary between hospitality and the horizon. International orange and park green carry the spirit of Tokyo Tower and Shiba Park into the renewed upper-floor suites and social spaces, grounding the guest experience in the city’s most iconic panoramic landscape.
editorial:
The Prince Park Tower Tokyo occupies a distinctive position in the capital. From its upper floors, Tokyo Tower rises in close proximity above the mature greenery of Shiba Park, bringing together two enduring aspects of the city: its metropolitan identity and its quieter landscape of gardens, temples and public spaces.
For the hotel’s twentieth anniversary, Mitsui Designtec renewed the 32nd and 33rd floors around this relationship. The concept, “THE TOKYO FUSION,” carries the colour, light and cultural character of the surroundings into the restaurants, bar, Club Lounge and five suites. The result is closely tied to its address, giving international visitors an immediate connection with Tokyo while offering local guests a fresh perspective on a familiar landmark.
Tokyo Tower has shaped the visual culture of the city since 1958. At this proximity, its international orange becomes part of the interior atmosphere, reflected through rust, amber and warm accent tones. Shiba Park contributes greens, earth colours and a gentler spatial register. Their presence changes throughout the day as sunlight, weather and evening illumination alter the relationship between the rooms and the view. This sensitivity to time is central to the hospitality experience. Breakfast, afternoon work, dinner and late-night drinks each carry a different pace. Mitsui Designtec has organized the upper floors around these changing patterns, allowing the interiors to move naturally between social activity, private conversation and moments of rest.
In the principal restaurant, the central kitchen provides an interior focal point equal to the Tokyo skyline. Set beneath a dark suspended canopy, it concentrates the movement, heat and precision of food preparation at the centre of the room. At the same time, perimeter seating maintains a direct relationship with Tokyo Tower. Dark timber, stone and brass give the restaurant visual depth after sunset, when the illuminated city becomes the dominant field beyond the glass. Dining is shaped by two simultaneous performances: the making of the food and the changing light of Tokyo. The bar establishes a closer relationship with the city after dark. Bottles and glassware form a luminous line beneath the windows, accompanied by amber seating and deeper finishes. The skyline extends above the counter, contributing to the room’s colour and atmosphere. The setting captures a familiar Tokyo ritual: ending the day with a drink while watching the city continue beyond the glass.
During daylight hours, the dining rooms respond more closely to Shiba Park. Green upholstery, botanical patterns and pale stone surfaces carry the landscape into the interior through colour and texture. Slender furniture and lighting preserve the openness of the glazing, giving trees, sky and shifting weather a clear presence within the rooms. This connection introduces a welcome sense of calm at the centre of Tokyo. The expanded Club Lounge reflects the changing role of the contemporary city hotel. Guests arrive for breakfast, continue working, meet colleagues, hold private discussions, or stay longer between appointments. Window-side desks, lounge seating and enclosed meeting rooms support these routines within a coherent setting. The lounge serves as a temporary workplace, drawing room, and social space for travellers whose days span business, culture, and leisure.
The journey towards the guest rooms continues the hotel’s relationship with movement and view. Patterned flooring guides the upper-level corridors and leads to five renewed suites. Each suite has a distinct accent palette, while the principal living and sleeping spaces are oriented towards Tokyo Tower, Shiba Park and the wider city. Within the suites, living, dining, working and sleeping areas form a connected domestic landscape. Low furniture maintains open sightlines to the windows, while glass and stone extend the rooms' visual depth. Artwork, textiles and colour introduce contemporary cultural references at a scale suited to daily life. Orange and rust tones echo the warmth of Tokyo Tower in one suite, while greys, blues and greens respond to the sky and park in another.
The variation gives returning guests a different experience on each visit while maintaining a consistent sense of place. Every suite belongs to the same architectural story, yet each presents its own interpretation of life above Tokyo.
The renewal of The Prince Park Tower Tokyo positions hospitality as a way of experiencing the city. Food, work, conversation, rest, design, and art are brought together in a setting shaped by one of Tokyo’s most recognizable landmarks and one of its established green spaces. Mitsui Designtec has developed the upper floors as a contemporary portrait of the capital, guided by colour, programme and changing views.
Tokyo is encountered through the glow of the tower, the greenery of the park, the activity of the kitchen and the changing atmosphere of the rooms. The hotel becomes a place from which to observe the city and participate in its daily rhythm, offering guests a relationship with Tokyo that continues beyond the view itself.

excerpt: Nikken Sekkei redefines the hospitality experience at InterContinental Sapporo, synthesizing Hokkaido’s seasonal landscapes, Ainu cultural narratives, and curated residential design into a cohesive architectural statement.
editorial:
Sapporo is a city characterized by a distinctive transformation across seasons. Snow alters the urban scale in winter, while the return of vibrant greenery in summer enhances the city's aesthetic appeal. Beyond the urban grid, the surrounding mountains serve as a continual backdrop. Situated between Nakajima Park and the Toyohira River, the InterContinental Sapporo embodies the concept of "Maison des saisons," or "The Home of Seasons," as designed by NIKKEN SEKKEI.
 
The notion of home is of considerable significance. The hotel’s rooms are thoughtfully designed to evoke the essence of curated spaces, featuring handcrafted elements, classical furnishings, richly textured fabrics, and artworks that convey individual character. This residential quality infuses the interiors with a personal rhythm, complemented by the evolving landscape of Hokkaido, which contributes a broader narrative to the environment.
 
Natural themes permeate the hotel through references to water, fire, and forest, drawing from an Ainu understanding of a world imbued with spiritual presence. These thematic elements are manifested in various public spaces, transitioning from reflective surfaces and lush planting to warmer, hearth-like settings characterized by deeper tones. Cultural references are integrated through atmosphere, material selection, and spatial relationships.
 
At the reception area, water establishes the initial ambiance. The use of dark stone, reflective surfaces, and dense plant life creates a composed arrival experience that resonates with the external landscape. The pathway through the lobby resembles a stroll through a garden, with light, foliage, and textured surfaces encouraging a deliberate pace as one enters the hotel.
 
The library lounge embodies a contrasting character through the element of fire. Deep reds, darker timber, and low seating create an intimate environment conducive to conversation. Illuminated shelving and intricately crafted screens lend the room a familiar ambiance akin to a private salon. The shifts in colour and material reflect the changing temperament of the public areas while contributing to a cohesive seasonal narrative.
 
Additionally, the incorporation of planting and softer forms evokes a forest-like atmosphere within the hotel. Furniture is strategically placed among greenery, creating spaces that feel both collected and inhabited, allowing public areas to transition fluidly between café, lounge, and dining environments. The overall experience resembles a journey through a large residence with distinct moods rather than passing through conventional hotel zones.
 
The material and artistic selections within the hotel are informed by Hokkaido’s landscape. Natural textures, locally relevant colours, and works by regional artisans foster a nuanced connection to the geographical context. In the guestrooms, carpets abstract the landscape of adjacent Nakajima Park, while artwork, timber, and carefully curated furnishings continue the narrative of a residence influenced by its surroundings.
 
The hotel's orientation provides a broader horizon, with Nakajima Park and the Toyohira River readily accessible, and Mount Bankei present in the distance. Consequently, the impact of seasonal change remains evident beyond the hotel’s interior, reinforcing the concept of a property whose character is intricately connected to the landscape throughout the year.
 
The Club Lounge further develops the residential theme through a lighter colour palette and a curated collection of art, furniture, and objects arranged for dining and conversation. The bar creates a richer evening atmosphere, where warm red and gold artwork, dark timber, and illuminated bottles offer an alternative interpretation of Hokkaido’s seasonal colours.
 
Throughout the InterContinental Sapporo, NIKKEN SEKKEI approaches regional identity as an experience that accumulates through materiality, art, landscape, and evolving atmosphere. "Maison des saisons" provides the hotel with a narrative language that aligns with the essence of Sapporo: urban in context, intimately connected to nature, and shaped by the rhythms of a place where each season reveals a new perspective.

excerpt: MIGIRI Design redefines Ginza wine culture with Salon du vin ivresse. A masterclass in stone, washi, and hidden light, this interior creates a secluded sanctuary for wine appreciation five floors above the city.
editorial:
Five floors above Ginza 7-chome, the salon du vin ivresse is designed as a place to relax with wine and let the hectic pace of the district fade away. MIGIRI Design has crafted the experience around the concept of "ma," focusing on space, silence, and carefully controlled lighting to enhance small sensory shifts: the aroma, temperature, the movement of a glass, and the lingering sensations that follow tasting.
 
The interior is structured to highlight these moments of awareness. A deep green stone serves as the backdrop for the counter, evoking the colour of a vineyard, while rows of bottles create a visual rhythm. Across the room, washi artwork captures and diffuses light through its fibres, subtly changing as illumination shifts throughout the day.
 
Natural materials like stone, timber, and washi, along with indirect lighting, are used with restraint. Light sources are concealed, allowing surfaces to emerge through reflection and shadow. MIGIRI Design describes this as a careful balance between what should be illuminated and what can remain subdued, giving each seat a slightly different relationship with the room.
 
The arrival sequence introduces a sense of control. An abstract artwork near the entrance establishes a threshold before the counter comes fully into view, with a straightforward and direct circulation path. Gradated wall tones adjust the atmosphere from seat to seat, and artwork alongside the windows incorporates the neighbouring cityscape as "borrowed scenery," ensuring Ginza remains present at the edge of the experience.
 
The service area is compactly planned, allowing the bar to maintain its density while meeting practical needs for storage, preparation, and guest circulation. The washroom continues the same material language, keeping the experience consistent from arrival to departure.
 
The name "ivresse," meaning intoxication, reflects a quieter side of wine culture. The focus is on the moments before tasting, the deepening sensations afterward, and the way time can seem to stand still during an evening. MIGIRI Design provides an architectural framework for these moments through the arrangement of bottles, the way light is absorbed by washi, and the solidity of stone.
 
Salon du vin ivresse transforms a small Ginza wine bar into a study of duration, atmosphere, and sensory focus, where the experience of wine is shaped as much by silence and materials as by what is poured into the glass.

excerpt: Park Homes Shijo Kawaramachi blends 400 years of temple heritage with contemporary residential design. Mitsui Designtec incorporates Nishijin-ori textiles, Kyoto's garden culture, and grid-based architecture to create a functional gallery for daily communal living.
editorial:
At Park Homes Shijo Kawaramachi, Mitsui Designtec draws inspiration from the rich cultural fabric of Kyoto to shape the communal experience of a modern residence. The building is located next to a temple with a history spanning four centuries, and its shared interiors incorporate elements of Nishijin weaving, seasonal flowers, literature, garden culture, and the city's historic street grid.
 
The communal areas are designed as a private “Gallery of Kyoto.” Art, crafts, and local references are integrated into the residents’ daily pathways through the building, giving the common spaces a cultural identity that evolves over time with repeated use.
 
A striking glass art installation marks the double-height entrance. This piece incorporates ro, the open gauze traditionally used for summer kimonos, and transforms its lightness into a suspended composition of fibre, glass, and gold. Viewed from the entrance, staircase, and upper landing, the installation changes with different perspectives and light conditions, bringing a sense of movement to the atrium through shifting transparency and reflection.
 
Stone, dark metal, and timber create a subtle backdrop for this artwork. Beneath the stairs, rocks and gravel form a dry landscape that connects the entrance to Kyoto’s temple and garden traditions through both material choice and composition. On the second floor, the communal program is organized around three themes: IKOU, TSUTAU, and MANABU, which translate to relax, inherit, and learn. IKOU features a lounge space for conversation and relaxation. TSUTAU showcases contemporary Nishijin-ori and local crafts. MANABU provides an environment for reading that includes books, ceramics, and references to Kyoto’s cultural history.
 
Nishijin-ori also influences the spatial layout. The interplay of warp and weft is reflected in lattice screens that filter views between connected areas. Their layered design allows light and movement to flow across the floor while creating a clear sense of enclosure for each space. Kyoto’s goban-no-me, the historic grid that has shaped the city for centuries, is echoed in the alignment of floors, shelves, and partitions within the interior. This consistent geometry allows the unique characteristics of stone, timber, textiles, and artwork to shine through.
 
MANABU organizes books, ceramics, and artworks in a tranquil setting suited for reading and close observation, while IKOU offers a more residential atmosphere. Loose seating, natural light, and floral arrangements make it a relaxed space for residents to unwind outside their apartments. Seasonality is also a significant consideration. Flowers and branches are incorporated into the lattice and along circulation routes, reflecting Kyoto’s longstanding tradition of marking the seasons with thoughtfully chosen arrangements.
 
The project also embraces okuyukashisa, a sensibility associated with discretion, depth, and refinement. Artworks, objects, and materials can be discovered from various distances and through layered views, providing a sense of exploration that unfolds over time. Park Homes Shijo Kawaramachi integrates Kyoto’s craft traditions, literature, and seasonal culture into contemporary residential life. Mitsui Designtec weaves these references into the daily experiences of the building, establishing a strong connection between its shared spaces and the cultural essence of the city.

excerpt: TOCLAS SALON TOKYO redefines the retail experience by bridging brand storytelling with technological precision inside a stunning, sustainable timber-hybrid space designed by Mitsui Designtec.
editorial:
In Tokyo's Kyobashi district, the traditional showroom experience, often filled with price lists and cabinetry dimensions, is changing significantly. TOCLAS SALON TOKYO, designed by Mitsui Designtec, focuses on brand storytelling as a key pathway to product discovery. This flagship space encourages visitors to connect with the TOCLAS worldview before they even consider the practicalities of the products. 
Mitsui Designtec has structured this journey through a purposeful two-zone sequence. Upon entering, the Entrance Lounge sets the stage for important brand values like Surprise, Inspiration, Peace of Mind, and Timelessness. This emotional grounding prepares visitors for the Exhibition Area, where technical innovations take center stage. This flow guides visitors from an initial impression of the brand to a deeper understanding of its product capabilities. 
The design of the space plays a vital role in this experience. Situated within the Kyobashi Kinoterrace, the salon reflects the building's exposed timber-and-steel framework. These wooden beams serve as the primary design language, showcasing the brand’s commitment to sustainability. By highlighting the structural framework, Mitsui Designtec ensures the salon has a clear identity based on material honesty and avoids a cluttered appearance. 
This design approach elevates the visit from a simple transaction to an engaging brand experience. Brand identity provides essential context, while the technical displays illustrate how this philosophy fits into everyday domestic life. In this environment, architecture lends credibility, the atmosphere draws attention, and technology enriches the design narrative, demonstrating how a manufacturer can connect seamlessly with modern living.

excerpt: KOKUYO transforms UACJ headquarters into a high-performance workspace utilizing structural aluminum loops. This design integrates corporate branding with circular economy principles and fluid employee movement to drive business innovation.
editorial:
At UACJ's newly relocated headquarters in Tokyo, aluminum is used to express the company's identity without relying on traditional corporate displays. KOKUYO works closely with UACJ to weave together fabrication, recycling, and workplace culture into a unified architectural story. The project revolves around the theme “Connect RING — Connecting and Being Connected.” Visitors experience this concept through a series of actions rather than a simple graphic. Upon arrival, they receive a canned drink, discover UACJ’s products, participate in meetings, and return the empty can for recycling before they leave. This familiar action serves as an introduction to the material cycle that is central to UACJ's business.
 
Aluminum shapes the character of the entrance space. Reception elements, benches, perforated surfaces, and integrated details were collaboratively crafted with UACJ artisans, showcasing the precision of bending, joining, and finishing. The headquarters highlights industrial knowledge through craftsmanship instead of typical product displays.
 
The collaboration between designer and manufacturer is essential to this project. KOKUYO integrates UACJ’s technical expertise into the design process, allowing the company’s material to contribute to furniture, architectural elements, and lighting. The entrance embodies the confidence that comes from a deep understanding of aluminum, from its production to its application. Beyond the visitor area, the principle shifts from material to movement. A continuous pathway connects work areas, meeting rooms, and informal spots, making it easy for employees to navigate the space and encouraging interactions among different teams throughout the day.
 
About 150 meters of linear lighting runs along this pathway, helping people understand the layout without adding extra walls or signs. Curved benches, circular tables, and casual meeting spots appear at various intervals, giving the design a human scale where people can pause, talk, and work. Open work areas are designed to be practical and flexible, with desks complemented by quieter zones along the brighter perimeter. Shared tables, plants, and informal seating provide places for quick chats, short tasks, or meetings without the need for a reserved room. This layout accommodates various activities without isolating them into separate environments.
 
The connection between the visitor experience and the workspaces comes from a consistent theme of interaction. At the entrance, this is expressed through aluminum, manufacturing, and recycling. Inside the office, it shows through movement, visibility, and the shared use of space.
 
UACJ’s headquarters embodies a clear corporate identity. KOKUYO builds on the company’s material expertise, manufacturing culture, and everyday workplace relationships to create an environment where “Connect RING” is experienced rather than just stated.

metadata.Project type: Interior Design — Hotel and Resort / Rebranding and Renovation

excerpt: Nagoya's hospitality scene transforms with the BASE LAYER HOTEL. MITSUI Designtec has revamped a landmark property into a high-performance 'Culture Business Hotel,' merging private sauna suites, immersive media areas, and modular urban living for today's traveller.
editorial:
BASE LAYER HOTEL NAGOYA NISHIKI reimagines the traditional business hotel format by giving it a broader cultural role. MITSUI Designtec's renovation of this 22-year-old property aims to create a space that caters to work, rest, media consumption, wellness, and a deeper connection to the city—all encapsulated under the concept of a “Culture Business Hotel.” The name "Base Layer" hints at its purpose. A base layer is the first item worn, close to the body, designed to support everything that follows. Similarly, the hotel prioritizes essentials like sleep, bathing, storage, and work, then enhances these elements through colour, art, technology, and sauna culture.
 
This approach is ideal for short urban stays. A guest may arrive for business, spend an evening streaming a film, use the laundry facilities, book a sauna, socialize with friends nearby, and leave the next morning without any of these activities competing for attention. Each has enough space to feel intentional.
 
The renovation focuses on the areas that guests frequent the most. The entrance is accentuated with a dark stone base, an illuminated canopy, and a deep green threshold, while the reception area adopts this palette in a subtler way. Timber ceilings, dark counters, and long built-in seating establish a sense of order without overcrowding the space. Green is a recurring theme throughout the project. It can be found in upholstery, corridor walls, shower enclosures, signage, and selected joinery, giving the hotel a recognizable identity across various spaces. This controlled use of colour also serves as a navigation aid within the retained building.
 
Guest rooms are compact but thoughtfully planned. Beds, storage, work surfaces, and bathrooms are arranged with minimal wasted space, while pale timber, warm grey, and black metal maintain a restrained visual language. Larger Japanese-style rooms offer low seating, kitchenettes, and more flexible floor space, accommodating families, groups, and longer stays. One notable feature is the green shower booth. Its translucent enclosure provides visibility within the room, transforming a functional aspect into a part of the brand's identity. Privacy is available when needed, while the glass maintains an open and airy feel.
 
The rooms also reflect how guests spend their downtime today. Large screens, shelves, pegboards, and graphic panels support streaming, gaming, and the use of personal devices, ensuring the room feels modern without conforming to a specific lifestyle image. Wellness also plays a significant role in the hotel's identity. Selected suites include private löyly saunas with cold bathing, integrated into the overall experience. Bookable sauna rooms extend this wellness ritual throughout the building, with heat, cold, and recovery processes organized around "totonou," the Japanese practice of physical and mental reset.
 
This program adds value beyond simple accommodation. The sauna can become a compelling reason to stay, while comfortably coexisting alongside the practical aspects of work, laundry, and media use.
 
The retained building also contributes to the project's character. Existing hardware and infrastructure are preserved where feasible, with investments focused on surfaces, equipment, and functions that enhance daily use. This approach results in a focused renovation that respects the building’s original structure while providing a new identity through selective changes.
 
BASE LAYER HOTEL NAGOYA NISHIKI combines the efficiency of a business hotel with a broader vision for urban stays. MITSUI Designtec has integrated work, rest, local culture, digital life, and sauna traditions within one cohesive framework, giving the hotel a contemporary relevance that goes beyond just an overnight stay.

metadata.Project type: Interior Design — Commercial and Office / Compact Workplace

excerpt: KOKUYO Co., Ltd. optimizes the ASOOM Shimbashi office by integrating traditional Japanese residential architecture to maximize compact commercial space. This project demonstrates how the *irori* hearth and central courtyards enhance productivity and foster social connections in high-density Tokyo work environments.
editorial:
In a city where work and domestic life increasingly overlap, ASOOM Shimbashi explores a workplace model inspired by the social intelligence of Japanese homes. Designed by KOKUYO for a Japanese homebuilder, this project integrates work, dining, socializing, and relaxation within a compact Tokyo setting, utilizing familiar residential concepts to foster a more adaptable office culture.
 
The central idea, “Office as a Home,” is expressed through a series of spatial references deeply rooted in Japanese domestic life. Elements such as the *irori* (a traditional fireplace), courtyards, *noren* curtains, and *fusuma* sliding doors are reinterpreted based on their original purposes of gathering, ventilation, filtered light, and adjustable privacy.
 
The courtyard plays a crucial role on the third-floor office level. In traditional narrow houses, these spaces once brought light, air, and glimpses of nature into the home’s core. KOKUYO translates this concept to the workplace by arranging desks to ensure that greenery remains visible throughout the floor. The intention is not merely to use plants as decoration but to establish a shared visual focal point and to foster a quieter relationship with the bustling city outside.
 
The basement common area draws inspiration from the *irori*, which was once the social heart of a Japanese home. In this contemporary setting, it becomes a space where colleagues and visitors can gather informally, with the surrounding area designed to adapt between conversation, reading, events, and collaborative work. A sense of community is created through proximity and flexibility, rather than by assigning each activity to a separate room.
 
This flexibility extends through softer forms of enclosure. Sheer curtains and bookshelves can be rearranged in the basement to suit various uses, referencing the adjustable boundaries traditionally associated with *noren* and *fusuma*. KOKUYO incorporates these design elements as functional aspects, allowing the office to transform throughout the day while maintaining an overall sense of coherence.
 
Material selection enhances this sense of familiarity. Timber, rattan, and hemp-inspired textures and surfaces chosen for direct physical contact give the workplace a warmer, more tactile character. Turned-wood offcuts are used in table edges, extending the life of discarded materials while improving comfort for drawing and daily tasks.
 
For workplace design, this project signifies a broader shift in how compact offices can accommodate various states of attention and interaction. A communal table can serve both work and meals; a curtained area can promote focus or host events; and a planted courtyard can provide both orientation and visual respite. The office becomes easier to navigate because its spaces are not bound to a single rigid function.
 
ASOOM Shimbashi gives “Office as a Home” a distinctly Japanese foundation. KOKUYO translates concepts like the courtyard, *irori*, and gentle domestic thresholds into a contemporary workplace, facilitating movement between work, conversation, and rest, and incorporating the rhythms of everyday life into the heart of the office.

metadata.Project type: Interior Design — Commercial and Office / Common-Area Renovation

excerpt: JA KYOSAI SAITAMA BUILDING has undergone a common-area overhaul by MITSUI Designtec, which optimizes corporate workflow through lighting-driven design and flexible community zones within a 50-year-old structural framework.
editorial:
After more than fifty years of use, an office building develops its own unique habits. For the renovation of JA KYOSAI’s Saitama office, MITSUI Designtec focuses on these shared routines, transforming the common areas to herald a new era for an established workplace.
 
The project is described as “new traditional,” a phrase that resonates with an organization whose identity is rooted in continuity. MITSUI Designtec preserves the building’s sense of order and institutional presence while introducing spaces that reflect the increasingly fluid nature of office life. Formal meetings remain important, but so do the moments before and after them, as well as the need for informal workspaces away from the desk.
 
This transformation begins in the atrium. The double-height lobby maintains its composed and symmetrical design, yet timber accents, mirrored surfaces, and a tall illuminated feature bring a lighter rhythm to the existing space. Seating is integrated into the area, transforming arrival into a setting where people can comfortably wait, meet informally, or spend a few moments between engagements.
 
Lighting plays a crucial role throughout the renovation. At the entrance, a broad illuminated frame provides the building with a distinctive evening presence. Inside, light is skillfully used to enhance height, depth, and movement, bringing greater definition to spaces whose proportions were established decades ago. This approach allows the architecture to retain its familiarity while altering how it is perceived and used.
 
The third-floor conference area exemplifies one of the more contemporary aspects of the project. The space outside the meeting rooms is designed for collaborative use with communal tables and benches, recognizing that office activities often extend beyond formally bookable rooms. Preparation, follow-up discussions, and brief periods of individual work can occur in this area, thereby increasing the utility of a space previously primarily associated with circulation.
 
The relatively low ceiling becomes part of the interior character. Coffered sections, linear pendants, and indirect lighting draw attention along the length of the space, while timber and upholstered seating create a work lounge ambiance. The design responds to the existing architecture through proportion and lighting rather than extensive reconstruction.
 
The basement Community Plaza introduces a different pace to the workday. Featuring plantings, green tiles, timber, and a variety of seating options, this area serves as a setting for lunch, conversation, individual work, or a brief break away from the main office floors. An expanded-metal screen marks the entrance, offering glimpses of movement beyond while providing a degree of separation without isolating it from the rest of the building.
 
Across these spaces, furniture plays a significant role in effecting change. Sofas, counters, communal tables, and benches present different seating options and lengths of use, allowing employees to choose how and where they spend their time between formal tasks. This flexibility complements the more structured architectural framework of the existing office.
 
Additionally, there’s a broader workplace narrative in the decision to prioritize common spaces. Corporate interiors are often defined by desks, meeting rooms, and technology, but much of an organization’s culture is shaped elsewhere: at the entrance, around shared tables, and in the moments between scheduled meetings. MITSUI Designtec emphasizes these in-between moments, giving them a clearer role in JA KYOSAI’s daily life.
 
In essence, “new traditional” describes a dynamic relationship between continuity and contemporary usage. The Saitama office retains the presence of an institution that has been at this location for fifty years, while its shared spaces take on a more social and adaptable character. This renovation allows the building’s history to remain visible, even as the everyday working life continues to evolve around it.

excerpt: A vertical garden bar in Ginza brings together Saint-Louis crystal, ancient cedar, and stone, establishing a new luxury hospitality, designed by A.N.D. NOMURA Co., Ltd.
editorial:
The collaboration between Saint-Louis and chef Kei Kobayashi in Ginza brings together two distinct worlds where time, precision, and craftsmanship are paramount. One world is embodied by the exquisite crystal made in the renowned furnaces of France, while the other reflects the meticulous hospitality and discipline of Japanese dining. At ST LOUIS BAR by KEI, A.N.D., NOMURA Co., Ltd. has created a unique architectural space that seamlessly transitions from an intimate bar to a sky garden.
 
The interior design draws on the Japanese concept of teioku ichinyo, which understands architecture and garden as a continuous composition. On the twelfth floor, this relationship begins inside, where stone, timber, plants, and crystal create their own landscape. This experience continues through the staircase and onto the rooftop, unfolding vertically through varying degrees of enclosure, light, and exposure to the city.
 
The choice of materials plays a significant role in the narrative. Date Kanmuri stone forms the central counter, maintaining the rock's irregularity and geological presence within a refined hospitality setting. Jindai cedar introduces a different sense of age; preserved over time before being reclaimed and worked, the timber brings dark grain and depth to the interior. Saint-Louis crystal enhances this composition through its light and reflections, with its brilliance accentuated by the subtler materials surrounding it.
 
When placed together, these three materials exemplify distinct forms of craftsmanship. Stone holds the history of the earth, cedar represents the passage of natural time, and crystal illustrates the transformation of raw materials through exceptional human skill. A.N.D., NOMURA Co., Ltd. allows these qualities to remain distinct, creating a setting where French decorative craftsmanship and Japanese material culture coexist closely.
 
The bar itself introduces another dimension of craftsmanship. A double-counter arrangement enables separate working spaces for bartenders, service staff, and pâtissiers while fostering a close connection with guests. This layout brings the precision of fine dining into the social atmosphere of a bar, where preparation, finishing, and service become integral to the evening without transforming the space into a performance stage.
 
This relationship is particularly relevant to Kei Kobayashi’s involvement. Food, drink, objects, and service are considered within a unified hospitality experience, giving even the smallest details on the counter significance. Saint-Louis crystal appears on an intimate scale through individual lights, vessels, and selected pieces, highlighting the brand's renowned qualities: clarity, cut, colour, and the way crystal responds to light.
 
The garden introduces a slower rhythm. A symbolic tree rises within the interior landscape, while plants lead to sculptural stairs composed of stone-like forms. The ascent extends the bar beyond the room itself, gradually opening the setting to air, weather, and the wider city.
 
Above, the rooftop serves as another interpretation of teioku ichinyo. Plants, stone, and low seating create an elevated garden where the atmosphere shifts with the seasons and times of day. A smaller pavilion provides a more enclosed experience within this landscape, with crystal lighting maintaining the connection to Saint-Louis while allowing the rooftop to develop its unique character.
 
The private lounge introduces a different mood through dark walls, leather, timber, and a suspended lattice overhead. Crystal pendants adorn this more sheltered area, bringing the material into a warmer, more residential context. Throughout the various spaces, repetition is avoided in favour of variation; the same cultural and material references take on different meanings based on how each section of the bar is utilized.
 
The choice of materials also reflects their origins. Certified domestic timber, reclaimed wood, and locally sourced hinoki are used alongside rooftop planting, addressing questions of sourcing and reuse within a project strongly focused on craftsmanship and longevity.
 
At ST LOUIS BAR by KEI, the collaboration between Saint-Louis, Kei Kobayashi, and A.N.D., NOMURA Co., Ltd. unfolds across multiple scales of craft: from the cutting of crystal to the preparation of food and drink, the working of timber and stone, and the cultivation of a garden above Ginza. Architecture provides the backdrop where these disciplines converge, guiding the evening from the intimacy of the counter to the changing light and seasons of the rooftop.

excerpt: A-Residence, designed by A.N.D. and NOMURA, redefines luxury living in Tokyo, merging dramatic book-matched marble, bespoke timber joinery, and museum-quality art against the backdrop of the iconic Tokyo Tower skyline.
editorial:
A-Residence exemplifies how various elements can be curated to create a tranquil environment. Located at a considerable height above Tokyo, with a view of Tokyo Tower at night, this residence showcases many features of contemporary luxury, including high-quality stone, custom joinery, bespoke furniture, curated art collections, and an impressive urban panorama. A.N.D., NOMURA Co., Ltd., applies a high degree of discipline to these elements. The project initiated with the living area and expanded into a comprehensive renovation, guided by ongoing collaboration with a client whose lifestyle spans multiple locations. The result is a thoughtfully constructed atmosphere in which materials, art, and views are in balance.
A notable aspect of this design is found at the entrance. A pine-themed artwork is positioned at the center of a dimly lit gallery, suspended above hand-carved stone vessels with polished surfaces reminiscent of still water. A circular opening of light highlights the composition, while the skyline of Tokyo glimmers beyond the window. This scene combines elements of installation art with the traditional function of an entrance, modifying the visitor’s pace. In just a few steps, the city remains visible, yet its noise is replaced with shadows, textures, stone, and the silhouette of a tree.
This sense of control extends throughout the residence. The open living and dining area possesses significant scale, yet it does not feel overly grand. Low-profile furniture maintains a grounded center of gravity, while timber walls add warmth to the space. A large stone dining table provides enough visual weight to stand confidently next to the skyline, and a suspended light fixture moves gracefully within the room. Though Tokyo Tower can be seen through the glazing, the interior does not solely frame the view; the architecture establishes its own visual rhythm, integrating the city into the overall composition.
Stone plays a central role in this design. A.N.D. carefully selected marble from raw blocks, developing its placement across floors and columns through extensive book-matching techniques. This decision is important, as the material is treated with the scale of architecture, rather than being applied as isolated decorative features. The veining flows across large surfaces, wraps around structural elements, and changes character as light interacts with the space. The designers refer to stone as forming a landscape, a term that is fitting in this context. Its natural patterns create a secondary topography within the residence that engages in a quiet dialogue with the metropolitan landscape outside.
Timber and washi paper introduce a softer tonal quality amidst the material intensity. Doors and storage solutions are integrated into expansive planes of joinery, allowing the wood grain to remain continuous while the architecture recedes when necessary. Smaller objects are displayed in illuminated niches, while larger artworks occupy generous wall spaces; furniture is positioned with the assurance of pieces intended for long-term placement. Art retains its significance without becoming an imposition on daily life. The residence conveys the notion that these objects belong to an individual, and that the spaces will continue to acquire meaning through use.
This perspective enhances the appeal of A-Residence. Luxury is often expressed through the accumulation of materials and objects.  Moreover, the project addresses the concept of ownership over time with thoughtful consideration. The client's existing furniture and cherished artworks were preserved and relocated alongside newly commissioned pieces. Marble was procured in block form and utilized consistently throughout the residence, allowing for natural variation to be incorporated into the design while minimizing waste. These choices contribute to a sense of sustainability grounded in longevity, continuity, and attachment: materials are selected for durability, and possessions with established histories are incorporated as integral components of the home.

excerpt: A.N.D. NOMURA Co. is transforming GORAKADAN FUJI GOLF into a year-round wellness resort that integrates professional golf facilities, hot springs, suites, and direct views of Mount Fuji.
editorial:
Golf clubs have long been places where rituals take shape: arriving early, changing attire, spending hours outdoors, returning to the clubhouse, and sharing conversations that linger in the air. At GORA KADAN FUJI GOLF, these time-honored practices are reimagined through a uniquely Japanese lens of retreat, with the majestic presence of Mount Fuji enhancing the experience from dawn to dusk.


This project revitalizes an established golf club situated next to the soon-to-be-completed GORA KADAN FUJI hotel, transforming the traditional clubhouse into a resort-like environment. While golf remains a focal point, the experience is elevated by the integration of natural hot springs, all-day dining, cozy fireside lounges, and luxurious suite accommodations. This thoughtful combination reflects a holistic view of leisure, where sports, hospitality, and relaxation seamlessly coexist.


The most striking aspect of GORA KADAN FUJI GOLF is, without doubt, Mount Fuji itself, which is prominently visible from the site. The architecture is meticulously designed to embrace this iconic backdrop, influencing the orientation and proportions of the shared spaces. Guests are afforded numerous opportunities to engage with this landscape, which holds a significance that transcends mere tourism.


This deep connection to the surrounding natural beauty redefines the clubhouse experience. Even though golf is the initial draw, the day's activities extend far beyond the final hole. Guests may find themselves soaking in rejuvenating hot springs, enjoying a meal with breathtaking views of the mountain, or gathering around a warm fire, all contributing to a slower pace more in line with Japanese resort culture. The architectural renewal pays tribute to the legacy of the original club, retaining elements of the existing structure and brickwork while introducing culturally resonant materials like Japanese stone and timber.


Throughout the interior, historical golf clubs and archival photographs are prominently displayed, ensuring that the building's past is woven into its new context. This layering of history adds a unique depth to the project. Golf was introduced to Japan as an imported sport, bringing with it Western clubhouse conventions. At GORA KADAN FUJI GOLF, these traditions exist alongside Japanese principles of spatial intervals, material restraint, and a deep appreciation of the natural world. This balance preserves both influences without allowing either to be reduced to mere decoration.


Integral to this design ethos is the Japanese concept of "ma," which emphasizes the importance of space between elements. Rooms are thoughtfully crafted to provide visual and physical room for the changing light, weather, and seasonal colors, inviting guests to fully appreciate the dynamic character of Mount Fuji. The mountain’s appearance shifts throughout the day, sometimes standing out in sharp relief, while at other times it melds into the surrounding atmosphere.


For the designers, the relationship between interior scale and landscape stands as a key achievement of the project. Symmetry offers balance, while carefully placed openings and intervals maintain a sense of fluidity. The use of timber, stone, and preserved brick creates interiors that have substance, enabling the distant mountain to remain the focal point. 


The clubhouse program is aligned with the rhythms of a full day. Arrivals, dining options, lounge spaces, suites, and terraces on the upper level all boast views of Mount Fuji, while the ground floor connects lockers and bathing facilities directly to the golf course. A new on-course teahouse provides an additional chance for reflection amid the game.


Importantly, the clubhouse’s accessibility has evolved as well. Certain dining and lounge areas are now open to the public, extending an invitation beyond the golfing community, while accommodations maintain a more intimate feel. This enhances the building’s role within the destination and strengthens ties to the nearby GORA KADAN FUJI hotel. This choice reflects the changing landscape of contemporary leisure travel in Japan, where golf, bathing, dining, and admiration of the scenic beauty can coexist in harmony.

excerpt: At % Arabica Cairo Roastery, stacked Egyptian limestone functions as seating, circulation areas, and landscape elements, effectively intertwining the memory of local quarries with the precision characteristic of Japanese design by no.10, NOMURA Co., Ltd.
editorial:
At U-Venues in New Cairo, % Arabica’s flagship roastery draws inspiration from the memory of quarrying. The design, executed by no.10, NOMURA Co., Ltd., seamlessly merges the brand’s Kyoto-born minimalism with Egypt’s rich stone heritage, thereby establishing a café environment where architectural elements convey a sense of locality, rather than relying solely on decorative embellishments.


The interior is arranged in a terraced layout composed of 800-millimetre limestone modules that rise, recede, and overlap in a manner reminiscent of excavated terrain. This innovative design not only forms seating, counters, niches, and circulation paths but also creates an integrated material system. Consequently, the café is perceived as a cohesive landscape rather than merely a collection of furniture and individual rooms.


Texture plays an essential role in differentiating tactile and visual perceptions. Vertical surfaces are intentionally left with a rough, split finish, evoking the appearance of extracted stone, while horizontal surfaces are polished to a smooth finish, enhancing the experience of benches, counters, and pathways. This contrast enables a single stone to fulfill structural, tactile, and aesthetic functions.


The modular design facilitates a variety of engagement options for patrons. Visitors may choose to sit elevated above the floor, congregate on broad benches, find comfort in recessed niches, or navigate clearly designated pathways within the stone terraces. This diversity in height and depth creates multiple seating choices, allowing the interior to maintain visual tranquillity while catering to varying durations of patron visits.


The coffee preparation areas are integrated within the same topography. Roasting and barista stations are illuminated with brighter, more concentrated lighting, transforming the preparation process into a daily performance. Conversely, guest areas benefit from softer lighting, establishing a distinct separateness between active and relaxed spaces without the need for physical barriers. This lighting scheme enhances the overall functionality of the café while clarifying the differing purposes of the architectural zones.


Hand-carved hieroglyphs enrich the stone surfaces with additional meaning. These symbols represent actions associated with grinding, pouring, serving, and drinking, thus linking ancient graphic language with contemporary practices. Their significance is derived from their ability to translate current activities rather than serving solely as antiquated motifs.


Circulation within the space is strategically guided through variations in level, texture, and light. The terraced floor design promotes organic movement, while views of the roasting equipment and service counter provide orientation and awareness. Minimal signage is employed, allowing the architectural form itself to establish spatial hierarchy.


The project's commitment to local sourcing enhances its material narrative. Utilizing Egyptian limestone reduces transportation needs, while the monomaterial system facilitates the integration of furniture within the building, thereby minimizing replaceable components. The durability of the interior is rooted in this decision, which also contributes to its identity: a cohesive landscape crafted from a single locally sourced material, thoughtfully distinguished through craftsmanship.


The project’s distinguishing feature lies in the synthesis of two design cultures. Japanese precision is evident in the modularity, junctions, and lighting discipline, while Egyptian heritage is expressed through the mass, texture, and symbolic carvings. Rather than presenting these qualities as separate themes, they converge to create a functional topography that gives % Arabica a distinctive global identity while ensuring a strong connection to Cairo’s cultural landscape.

excerpt: RENS. NOMURA Co., Ltd. revitalizes the RIHGA Royal Hotel Osaka by bridging the building’s historic architectural legacy with contemporary Japanese craft. Drawing on the concept of "The Fusion of Traditional Beauty and Water," the design integrates flowing metalwork, Nishijin weaving, and calligraphic motifs to connect the hotel to its Nakanoshima riverfront setting and the city's broader social memory.
editorial:
Hotels often become a part of a city’s memory long before they are recognized as significant architecture. It becomes part of a city’s social landscape, shaped by generations of arrivals, celebrations, meetings and returns. RIHGA Royal Hotel Osaka belongs to this category. Its identity has developed alongside modern Osaka, giving the building a cultural presence that extends beyond the conventions of luxury hospitality.
In April 2025, the hotel began a new chapter as RIHGA Royal Hotel Osaka, Vignette Collection. The renewal by RENS. NOMURA Co., Ltd. connects IHG Hotels & Resorts’ international platform with the architectural legacy of Isoya Yoshida, whose work brought Japanese aesthetics and Western influences into a distinctive and enduring composition.
The hotel’s location on Nakanoshima provides the project with its strongest reference point. Set between the Dojima and Tosabori Rivers, the island developed through Osaka’s commercial and cultural exchange. Water carried goods and ideas through the city, while Nakanoshima grew into a district of civic institutions, art, business and public life. The hotel’s description as “Floating Nakanoshima” captures this relationship between architecture and geography.
“The Fusion of Traditional Beauty and Water” converts that setting into a contemporary hospitality experience. The river appears through reflection, texture, movement and light, expressed across metalwork, Nishijin weaving, projected imagery, flooring and calligraphy. The theme remains consistent while each craft and material contributes its own character.
At the entrance, slender metal pipes form a new architectural gate. Their varied lengths and positions create a changing surface that responds to daylight, illumination and the movement of guests. Finished by specialist craftspeople, the installation combines the precision of metalwork with the fluidity of water, giving the hotel a renewed presence within the Nakanoshima streetscape.
The experience of arrival continues in the lobby, where Isoya Yoshida’s proportions and Western-style detailing remain part of the hotel’s contemporary life. Restored mouldings and joinery sit alongside brass, timber, textile and new lighting. Each layer remains visible, allowing the building’s age and renewal to be read together.
Behind the reception counter, a Nishijin textile folding screen provides the principal cultural gesture. Created using Fukurashi-ori, a three-dimensional weaving technique, its raised and recessed surfaces respond to light throughout the day. The composition captures the energy and changing density of water through textile, bringing Kyoto’s weaving tradition into the daily rituals of arrival and welcome.
Its position within reception gives craft an active role in the hotel. Guests experience the work while checking in, meeting companions or pausing in the lobby. Cultural knowledge is encountered through use and proximity, connecting artisanal practice with the social rhythms of an international hotel.
This dialogue between inherited architecture and contemporary craft gives the renewal its depth. The hotel’s history remains present through proportion, material and detail, while new commissions introduce a fresh cultural perspective. Design supports continuity across generations, allowing long-standing guests and first-time visitors to recognize the building as both established and current.
The journey to the guest rooms shifts the atmosphere from the lobby's social scale to a more personal one. Projected moonlight and reflections across the corridor floor guide movement with a gentle visual rhythm. The sequence introduces a sense of calm before guests enter their rooms.
Inside, the design draws water into the quieter rituals of rest. Green and ochre flooring changes in density around the bed, creating the impression of a surface in motion. The hotel’s signature green, brass lighting, restored mouldings, and soft upholstery give the rooms a composed, residential character that connects to the public spaces.
Calligraphic works extend across the headboards. Art becomes part of the guest’s daily experience, encountered while reading, resting and waking. Across all formats, artwork, materials, and light establish continuity with the wider hotel narrative.
For international visitors, Japanese culture is experienced through a sequence of encounters. Metal craft marks the entrance, Nishijin weaving shapes reception, projected light guides the corridors and calligraphy accompanies the guest room. These elements become part of arrival, movement and rest, giving cultural expression a direct relationship with hospitality.
RIHGA Royal Hotel Osaka enters its next era as both a cultural address and a place to stay. Its renewal connects design, art, craft, and hospitality with the life of the city, presenting Osaka through the movement of water, the continuity of architecture, and the rituals shared between the hotel and its guests.

excerpt: Discover CEVEN LAB by NOMURA Co., Ltd., an innovative sensory hub in Nagano where 300 years of spice tradition meets modern collaborative prototyping. This unique interior transformation redefines co-creation through live blending and sensory design.
editorial:
For almost three centuries, Yawataya Isogoro has turned spice into part of Nagano’s cultural identity. Founded in 1736, the company grew alongside the flow of pilgrims visiting Zenkoji, where hospitality was expressed through small acts of preparation, explanation and exchange. CEVEN LAB carries this tradition into a contemporary business setting, giving aroma and taste a central role in how new ideas are discussed and developed.
Created by NOMURA Co., Ltd. within a former confectionery workroom and warehouse, the facility brings together a test kitchen, showroom, archive, office, and business lounge. Its purpose responds to the way Yawataya Isogoro now works. The company has completed more than 300 collaborations and develops products from close to 40 spice ingredients, often with partners in food, fashion, entertainment, and popular culture. A request may begin with a brand story, a fictional character or an atmosphere that has yet to find a flavour. CEVEN LAB gives those abstract conversations a physical form. Partners can move directly from an image, word or cultural reference to ingredient selection, blending, aroma and tasting. The process places sensory experience at the centre of collaboration, allowing people from different industries to build a common language through something immediate and memorable.
The Blend Kitchen is where this exchange becomes visible. Two curved timber counters bring Yawataya Isogoro’s specialists and visiting partners together at the same height, with ingredients and samples passing easily across the shared surface. The arrangement creates the informality of a working studio and the concentration of a kitchen, giving each participant a direct role in shaping the result.
Above the counters, a circular golden canopy establishes a clear centre within the open warehouse. Its metallic surface recalls the lid of Yawataya Isogoro’s familiar shichimi tin, while integrated light draws attention to the activity below. The gesture connects brand memory with present-day work, giving a practical blending area the sense of occasion associated with a shared table. The wider interior keeps the character of the former warehouse visible. White-painted ducts, tracks and services remain overhead, set against pale timber joinery, light flooring and precise gold details. The designer, Ms. Yuri Nakagawa, uses this contrast to express a working culture that values both inherited knowledge and active experimentation. The atmosphere feels open, bright and purposeful, suited to a place where ideas need to move quickly between conversation and production.
Knowledge is made accessible through the archive. Shallow drawers hold past products, ingredients, and collaborations, while nearby displays showcase spices through colour, texture, and origin. A visitor can trace an earlier project, examine the materials behind it and carry that reference directly to the Blend Kitchen. The company’s history serves as a practical resource for new development, kept close to the people who use it. Seven coloured modular tables bring a more flexible rhythm to the collaboration area. Their tones refer to the components of shichimi, while their movable format supports small discussions, workshops and live-streamed sessions. A pair of collaborators can work beside the windows, then join a larger group as the project develops. The space adapts to the scale of the exchange, giving creative work room to expand.
This flexibility reflects a contemporary form of hospitality. Visitors are welcomed into the process through tasting, handling, and discussion, with Yawataya Isogoro’s staff sharing their knowledge up close. A spoonful of spice, a change in aroma or a small adjustment to a blend can communicate more clearly than a long presentation. The experience turns product development into a cultural encounter shaped by attention, curiosity and trust.
CEVEN LAB also brings Nagano’s food culture into wider creative conversations. Collaborations with brands and cultural properties introduce shichimi to audiences who may first encounter it through fashion, entertainment or design. The local ingredients and blending techniques remain visible throughout the process, giving each new partnership a direct connection to the company’s place of origin and accumulated expertise. By adapting an existing warehouse, NOMURA Co., Ltd. has created a workplace that supports research, business, and cultural exchange within a single shared environment. The project gives a long-standing regional company the means to work with new partners while keeping its knowledge active and tangible, but also presents heritage as something practised in the present. Yawataya Isogoro’s archive, ingredients and blending traditions provide the foundation, while the open kitchen and collaboration spaces invite new interpretations. The future of the brand is shaped by the same essential gestures that have defined it for generations: selecting, blending, tasting, and sharing.

excerpt: NOMURA Co., Ltd. is transforming Osaka's urban gateway by integrating the retail interiors of GRAND GREEN OSAKA with Umekita Park through responsive kinetic art, strategic lighting, and immersive biophilic design.
editorial:
At GRAND GREEN OSAKA, the delineation between the shopping district, station concourse, and urban park has been purposefully softened. In the South Commercial Zone, NOMURA Co., Ltd. has designed the interior as an integral component of Osaka’s larger pedestrian landscape, where retail, food, art, and public circulation collaboratively exist within the same civic environment.
 
This development is situated within one of the city’s most prominent mixed-use projects, directly connected to Osaka Station and Umekita Park. This strategic positioning influences the character of the commercial floors, featuring spacious pathways, visually accessible entrances, and long vistas that guide the eye toward greenery, terraces, and adjacent public spaces. The overall experience is akin to traversing a neighbourhood rather than entering a conventional shopping center.
 
The integration of nature is articulated through both landscaping and artistic interpretation. In one atrium, hundreds of suspended reflective elements evoke the appearance of leaves suspended in mid-air. Their polished surfaces fragment the surrounding architecture, people, and shifting light, creating a dynamic canopy that continuously evolves as visitors traverse the space beneath it. Additionally, sweeping bands of illuminated vertical structures delineate graceful curves across the ceiling, introducing a rhythmic elegance to major circulation areas and offering a distinctive identity to the concourse from afar.
 
This relationship with the landscape is expressed through a vertical arrangement of four distinct themes: Mineral on B1, Grove on 1F, Breeze on 2F, and Daylight on 3F. Each level distinctly conveys its own atmosphere while preserving a coherent connection to the broader theme of nature inherent in the development. The lower floors are characterized by stone-like textures and deeper tones, while the middle levels incorporate plantings and more inviting materials. The upper circulation areas are defined by brighter surfaces and more open ceiling configurations.
 
The B1 level represents the vibrant energy of an urban market, featuring Time Out Market Osaka, along with various cafés and Japanese restaurants. This area showcases a darker, more dense interior, where exposed ceilings, warm pendant lighting, and graphic signage create a distinctly social environment. This contrasts effectively with the brighter retail floors above, offering a diverse range of experiences that include quick dining options, evening gatherings, as well as shopping for fashion, jewelry, and opportunities for leisurely browsing.
 
Art is seamlessly integrated at multiple scales. Reflective ceiling installations invigorate major public pathways, while sculptural elements are strategically positioned near restaurants and along quieter passageways. This thoughtful placement allows cultural expressions to become part of the daily movement within the complex, encountered while navigating between shops, awaiting appointments, or proceeding toward the park.
 
The external architecture further reinforces this integrative relationship. Landscaped terraces, planted borders, and pedestrian courts occupy the spaces between the commercial podium and surrounding towers, effectively extending the retail environment into the public realm of GRAND GREEN OSAKA. From within, glazed openings and garden views maintain this connection, while from the park, the commercial levels present an animated edge to the larger urban district.
 
The most noteworthy aspect of the South Commercial Zone is the harmonious coexistence of these varied elements. Luxury retail, restaurants, public art, landscaped courtyards, and major commuting pathways each maintain distinct identities without devolving into isolated destinations. NOMURA Co., Ltd. has crafted a commercial interior that actively engages with the life of the district, thus extending the experience of GRAND GREEN OSAKA from the park and streets into the spaces where individuals shop, dine, convene, and spend their leisure time.

excerpt: Deco Farmer Studio transforms a Hong Kong apartment into a high-impact residential design. By leveraging primary colour blocks, strategic joinery, and custom geometric surfaces, the layout redefines traditional living spaces into a gallery-focused interior.
editorial:
Colour establishes the rhythm of "A Chromatic Rhapsody" from the moment you enter. Designed by Hong Kong-based Deco Farmer Studio, the residence uses yellow, green, red, and blue as instruments of spatial identity. Each colour corresponds to a surface, object, or threshold, allowing this compact domestic interior to convey the energy of a much larger space.
The conventional living room is reimagined as an expansive foyer. A bicycle is showcased against a geometric tiled wall, transforming an everyday object into a work of art and introducing the owners through the items they use. This playful gesture also alters how the home is perceived: the entryway, display, and social spaces overlap from the beginning.
Throughout the shared areas, loose furniture and built-in elements follow the same colour scheme. Doors, cabinets, and shelves are each assigned distinct blocks of colour, while patterned surfaces highlight the junctions between them. The colour palette is vibrant, yet its application remains deliberate. Large planes create visual order, while smaller accents introduce movement and prevent the interior from settling into a singular decorative style.
This careful control is especially evident in the guest room, which is divided into a man cave and a walk-in wardrobe. A red feature screen separates the two areas without completely closing them off. Textured wall coverings and contrasting colours provide each side with a unique character, turning a practical division into one of the project’s most expressive sequences.
The design also recognizes the importance of release. As the layout moves toward the owners’ bedroom, the colour palette softens, and the pace slows. Calmer tones signal privacy and rest, completing the transition from the lively public areas to a more tranquil personal retreat. Thus, the chromatic narrative has a clear beginning, crescendo, and conclusion.
Deco Farmer Studio utilizes colour to reflect personality while maintaining everyday functionality. Storage is thoughtfully integrated, circulation paths are clear, and personal objects are intentionally placed within the overall composition. While the residence feels curated, it doesn’t resemble a showroom. Its most compelling quality is the sense that the colours have emerged from the owners’ habits, sense of humour, and appreciation for visual vibrancy.
"A Chromatic Rhapsody" presents domestic exuberance as a form of discipline. The project’s confidence stems from a clear understanding of where colour should dominate, where texture should add depth, and where quieter surfaces are needed. This balance transforms a bold palette into a livable environment and gives the home an immediate, personal identity that resonates throughout the entire space.

excerpt: NX DESIGN HOME transforms a multi-level family home into a masterclass of structural light and circulation. This private residence balances open-plan connectivity with high-performance spatial efficiency for a family of six.
editorial:
A house shared by six people naturally develops its own rhythm. Mornings revolve around breakfast and departures, afternoons see activities scattered across different rooms, and evenings bring the household back together. At Hollow Valley Residence, NX DESIGN HOME focuses on this daily routine, using daylight, expansive views, and a thoughtfully organized layout to keep a substantial family home connected without feeling over-managed.
 
The designers worked with a household that includes four children, which immediately shifts the priorities in a large residence. Generous space is beneficial, but only when it remains easy to navigate, adaptable, and capable of supporting multiple routines at once. Hollow Valley Residence is shaped around these realities. Communal areas remain visually open, circulation paths are clear, and storage is integrated into the architecture to accommodate change while maintaining composure.
 
Daylight sets the interior’s rhythm. Floor-to-ceiling glazing allows the atmosphere to transition from misty mornings to bright afternoons and the warm tones of evening. Columns, walls, and light surfaces register these shifts throughout the day, making the passage of time perceptible within the interior itself.
 
While this concept could have become purely decorative, NX DESIGN HOME maintains its architectural integrity. The structural columns are visible across the main living area, establishing a rhythm within the open plan and helping to delineate activities without relying on numerous walls. Their shadows change as the day progresses, giving the fixed structure a dynamic presence.
 
The kitchen bears much of the social responsibility of the house. Its elongated island combines storage and prep space with the informal function of being a family gathering point. Aligned with the cabinetry behind it, the island also helps organize movement throughout the wider communal area.
 
This distinction is vital in a family home. The kitchen is not treated as a display piece set apart from daily life; rather, it integrates into the household’s circulation, becoming a place where cooking, conversation, and movement naturally overlap. The design acknowledges that some of the most significant moments in a home occur in these ordinary interactions.
 
The restrained color palette allows routines to unfold naturally. Pale mineral surfaces, timber, glass, and muted upholstery create continuity throughout the residence, while variations in daylight offer visual interest. The overall effect is calm without feeling overly precious—an essential quality in a home expected to accommodate the unpredictability of family life.
 
Hollow Valley Residence becomes even more architecturally ambitious as it extends below ground. At the second basement level, glass is utilized to bring light deeper into the building, sustaining a visual connection with the levels above. The designers aimed to preserve a sense of linkage to above-ground life, even in the deepest areas of the house.
 
This thoughtful use of space adds significant depth to the residence. Brightness is not limited to the perimeter; it flows through openings, glazed boundaries, and framed views, allowing the lower levels to remain part of the same domestic environment.
 
This approach is particularly suited to a family home. As children grow, routines shift, rooms gain new purposes, and the household gradually reorganizes itself over time. NX DESIGN HOME has equipped Hollow Valley Residence with a structure capable of adapting to these changes while maintaining coherence.
 
Therefore, its strongest quality is not the stillness captured in photographs, but rather how the interior is designed for movement. Daylight shifts across the columns, people gather around the island, activities transition between floors, and the atmosphere transforms from morning to evening. Hollow Valley Residence is crafted around these recurring moments, providing a large family home with both spatial clarity and the flexibility to evolve.
