excerpt: Explore how NANJING SUKONG transforms a narrow townhouse into a vertically connected home. This project features a skylight-lit central staircase and a glass lift, maximizing light and spatial flow.
editorial:
In Zimo ● Songjing, light is integrated into the household as an essential element rather than just a finishing touch. NANJING SUKONG INTERIOR DESIGN CO. LTD. has transformed a traditional townhouse by introducing a new vertical sequence that allows daylight from a third-floor skylight to flow through the center of the home, connecting rooms that would otherwise feel like separate levels.
The transformation begins with the staircase, which has been reconfigured from two flights into three and paired with a transparent lift, making it the central feature of the residence. Daylight, movement, and glimpses of family life all pass through this vertical chamber, providing the house with a sense of internal orientation that is experienced from one floor to the next. The lift is an integral part of this architectural composition, carrying reflections and changing light throughout the day without obstructing the center of the layout.
The result is a home organized around relationships rather than isolated rooms. The basement, ground floor, and mezzanine support the more social aspects of daily life, while the upper levels are designated for bedrooms and private facilities. This gradual transition creates a natural rhythm throughout the house, moving from gathering and entertainment spaces to areas of rest and privacy, all while maintaining the visual continuity that unites the interior.
This continuity is particularly crucial in a multi-level home. While staircases typically function solely as a means of moving between floors, here they also allow family members to stay aware of activities happening elsewhere in the house. Sightlines across landings, openings that frame adjacent rooms, and light that travels vertically all contribute to a sense of connection within the domestic realm. The choice of materials is deliberately controlled. Light-colored surfaces reflect changing daylight, while darker cabinetry adds definition to the larger rooms. Warm red-brown tones introduce depth to the communal spaces. These elements establish continuity without flattening the individual character of each room. Living, dining, and transitional areas remain distinct yet are perceived as parts of a cohesive whole.
On the upper floor, the atmosphere becomes more personal. The third level is designed as a complete suite, where the architecture pays particular attention to the rituals of private life. An opening above the tatami area allows afternoon light to traverse textured walls, making the passage of time a visible component of the room. The master bedroom furthers this concept through its structure. Black beams and columns create a more intimate scale around the bed and incorporate the sloping roof into the design. Their presence stems from the structural renovation, giving the room a stronger architectural identity while allowing sleeping, storage, and tatami areas to coexist within one space.
Transparency is handled with equal thoughtfulness. Rippled glass blocks between the master bathroom and wardrobe allow light to permeate while maintaining privacy. In the south-facing bedroom, an acrylic screen separates sleeping and laundry functions by diffusion rather than complete enclosure. These materials keep adjacent activities connected through light, even when direct views are softened.
This approach gives the project relevance within contemporary residential design. Privacy is not merely viewed as a binary state of open or closed; instead, it can be modulated through translucency, distance, material choices, and varying levels of visibility. This same principle applies to the house as a whole: shared life remains perceivable without compromising the tranquil character of the upper floors.
NANJING SUKONG INTERIOR DESIGN CO. LTD. employs stairs, skylights, structural elements, and translucent boundaries to strengthen the relationship between everyday routines, light, and family interactions. The house becomes most expressive through the continually changing moments, such as a figure moving behind glass, afternoon sunlight crossing a wall, or an unexpected view opening between floors.

excerpt: Beijing Easy-Home sets a new standard in hospitality spatial design with RenownGarden Chongqing, creating a continuous flow using perforated metal, reflective surfaces, and precisely controlled lighting.
editorial:
RenownGarden Chongqing is defined by a distinctive tension between clarity and illusion. Beijing Easy-Home Interior Design Co., Ltd. establishes a precise architectural framework for this project, which is artfully disrupted through reflection, filtered light, and variations in transparency. The focus is less on decorative luxury and more on perceptual experiences and specifically, how a room transforms as one navigates through it, how a corridor may appear deeper than its actual dimensions, and how a surface can appear solid from one perspective while appearing nearly immaterial from another.


This design philosophy is most prominently illustrated in the cooler public areas. The integration of silvered glass, pale stone, and translucent panels creates an atmosphere that is both crisp and nearly weightless, while expansive glazing and reflected views maintain a connection to the external landscape. Light plays an integral role in shaping the spatial experience. Perforated metal screens diffuse points of illumination across walls and circulation routes, generating a layered depth that dynamically alters with the observer's position.


Consequently, the corridors fulfill a more significant function than is customary in hospitality projects; they become an integral aspect of the overall experience rather than mere conduits between different spaces. Repetition, reflection, and controlled brightness extend the visual field, while selected objects and artworks serve as focal points within the continuous flow of movement.


The application of blue accents is judicious, thereby enhancing their impact. Sculptural seating, vertical installations, and carefully chosen wall surfaces introduce a cooler chromatic scheme without overwhelming the neutral backdrop. In contrast to the metallic and translucent materials, these elements function as markers within the broader composition, enabling individual spaces to maintain their distinct identities while remaining visually cohesive.


A contrasting atmosphere is evoked in the bar and dining areas, where warm timber, bronze-toned screens, and darker ceilings replace the cooler luminosity with a more intimate ambiance. This transition is seamless; the same principles of perforation, reflection, and filtered light persist, but their temperature and density adapt to accommodate longer stays and facilitate private conversations.
The stairway is a vital transitional element between these two contrasting environments. Enclosed by tall glazing and metal screens, it receives abundant natural light during the day while preserving the project's emphasis on shadow, translucency, and layered views. Its folded geometry imparts a distinct architectural presence, allowing movement between levels to become an essential component of the spatial narrative.


Several quieter spaces within the project reveal an alternate aspect of the design. Pale upholstery, curated plant compositions, and soft blue walls create environments where reflective surfaces recede, allowing texture to take on greater significance. These areas introduce a more leisurely pace, enabling the interior to shift between visual intensity and restraint while maintaining coherence.


In conclusion, RenownGarden Chongqing is characterized by controlled variation. The project does not rely on a single dramatic space or a signature material. Instead, its identity is cultivated through consistent adjustments in opacity, light, colour, and enclosure. Beijing Easy-Home Interior Design Co., Ltd. effectively translates these variations into a cohesive spatial language, resulting in an interior that is most memorable in motion, where each change in angle uncovers a nuanced interpretation of the space.

excerpt: Muneji Toh Architects transforms industrial perforated sheet metal into dynamic pendant lighting using metal-spinning techniques. This process stretches the standard grid into custom geometries that project intricate, shifting light patterns across interior spaces.
editorial:
The Perforated Metal Spinning Lamp by Muneji Toh Architects is shaped by a small but consequential decision: to spin a sheet of metal after it has already been perforated.
Metal spinning is normally associated with smooth, controlled surfaces. In this case, the regular grid of openings is subjected to the same forming process as the metal itself. As the sheet is drawn into a three-dimensional shape, the perforations stretch with it, changing proportion according to their position on the curve. What begins as an industrially ordered surface becomes progressively less uniform as the form develops.
That change gives the lamp much of its character. The pattern isn't merely decorative surface ornament; it is the visible consequence of fabrication. The finished surface records how the material has moved, with the original perforation grid still legible beneath the distortions created by spinning.
When illuminated, those deformations become spatial. Light passes through openings of different shapes and projects an uneven field onto surrounding walls, making the effect of the process visible beyond the object itself. The shade therefore operates at two scales: as a compact pendant and as a source of changing light and shadow within the room.
There is also something useful in the tension between repetition and variation. The starting material is systematic, while the forming process introduces differences. Neither condition disappears completely. The lamp retains the discipline of an industrial product while allowing the behaviour of the material and the skill of the maker to remain visible.
For Muneji Toh Architects, the significance resides in this precise interplay between technique and form. Unburdened by extraneous motifs, the object relies entirely on its constituent act of making unifying structure, perforation, and illumination into a direct expression of industrial craft.

excerpt: Designed by KOKUYO Co., Ltd., Gateway Studio activates Takanawa Gateway City as a flexible public hub that utilizes modular, soil-inspired design to host community events, exhibitions, and localized information exchange.
editorial:
At Takanawa Gateway City, KOKUYO has redefined the role of the information center, positioning it as a dynamic space rather than merely a venue for announcements and orientation. Gateway Studio, strategically situated directly in front of the north ticket gates at Takanawa Gateway Station, was inaugurated in March 2025, in conjunction with the establishment of the new mixed-use district. This facility serves as a publicly accessible venue for information dissemination, events, exhibitions, pop-up shops, and community engagement. Its purpose is intimately connected to the ongoing development of a district that is still evolving: a locale where interests can be exchanged, relationships can be formed, and the identity of the new neighbourhood can be cultivated in a communal environment.
KOKUYO frames the project with the guiding principle “Nurture your ideas.” This agricultural metaphor informs both the conceptual and material dimensions of the studio. Within a district designed around rail infrastructure, offices, and urban development, the interior design draws inspiration from visual representations of fields, rice paddies, soil, and seeds. Dyed cork was created through the analysis of the local soil's coloration, while vibrant green seed-shaped pins are employed to secure posters, booklets, and other printed materials. As such, information is literally “planted” within the surfaces, integrating the act of display into the project's identity.
The concept is further expressed architecturally through shelving that encircles the core of the studio. Thick, ribbon-like surfaces finished in cork provide a robust horizontal structure while enhancing the available display area: items can be exhibited on both the upper and lower surfaces. Behind these shelves, mirror-finished steel introduces a reflective quality and serves as a magnetic surface for supplementary materials. Consequently, this fixture transcends mere storage; it functions as an adaptable communication framework where material, display, and concept are intricately interwoven.
This adaptability is extended through a series of cube-shaped mobile units. The cork faces permit the use of the same seed-shaped pins, perforated boards accommodate conventional hooks, and shelf boards of varied dimensions can be interspersed between the cubes to augment the display surface. Mounted on castors, these units may be rearranged within the studio or relocated outdoors to the adjacent plaza on favourable days, thus enabling exhibitions and information to align with the vibrant public life surrounding the building.
This mobility is critical to the project’s engagement with the city. The studio occupies a transparent pavilion that is surrounded by greenery and outdoor seating, ensuring that its boundaries remain visually and functionally permeable. Displays may extend toward the plaza, visitors can transition seamlessly between the interior and exterior, and the space can adapt to differing requirements from one day to the next. The architecture provides a stable framework, whereas the furniture allows for programmatic flexibility.
 
KOKUYO extends this design language into the graphics utilized throughout the studio. Imagery of seeds being sown into dark soil is prevalent across posters, signage, and products, thereby reinforcing the interior concept in the studio’s visual identity. Given that the facility must accommodate frequently changing information, this carefully curated vocabulary of soil, seeds, and uncomplicated geometry ensures that new content remains legible without resulting in visual disarray.
The Gateway Studio lies in how its design provides a tangible language for the evolving nature of public life. The cork surfaces capture the changing displays, the mobile fixtures traverse the room and plaza, and the graphic system maintains coherence between diverse activities. KOKUYO does not represent Takanawa Gateway City as a concluded urban product; rather, the studio is conceptualized around the idea that a new district accrues meaning progressively through the information, conversations, and small acts of participation that individuals contribute over time.

excerpt: Discover the SPARX Guest Area designed by KOKUYO. Observe live Nikkei 225 data and EDINET networks evolving into a dynamic, engaging environment. Investment strategies are made visible through data, art, and corporate hospitality.
editorial:
“This project is not just an office; it is a space that thinks.” This simple idea underpins the SPARX Guest Area & Lounge, designed by Tomoyuki Kobayashi of KOKUYO for the investment firm's headquarters. The design reflects the corporate philosophy that “the macro emerges from the accumulation of the micro.” The interior space serves as an active medium through which this concept can be perceived, heard, and physically experienced. The company introduces its identity through the visitor’s journey, embedding that identity in the experience.
The journey begins in a long reception area with white tones that overlooks Tokyo. Indirect lighting traces the edges of the ceiling, while pale surfaces diffuse daylight. A continuous timber bench follows the perimeter, gently curving around an indoor tree, creating a calm and unhurried atmosphere. Ornamentation is minimal, allowing light, proportions, and material textures to define the environment. A large digital artwork occupies one wall, presenting financial information in the soft form of a landscape rather than through traditional charts and trading screens.
This artwork is sourced from Japan’s EDINET system, a public database of corporate financial disclosures. Historical data is processed through a generative system inspired by the behaviour of slime mould, revealing connections between companies that might otherwise remain hidden. In this installation, numbers transform into colour, movement, and spatial relationships, making finance resemble a living ecology, where individual entities respond to one another within a continuously evolving system. This approach makes a complex subject more approachable without diminishing its sophistication, giving emotional weight to information typically understood through analysis alone.
A bronze-toned sliding threshold marks the transition from the reception area to a dark corridor. Its softly reflective surface captures a blurred image of the bright room before opening into shadow. The contrast is immediate: brightness gives way to darkness, stillness acquires rhythm, and the expansive reception narrows into a focused passage. This sequence operates with cinematic precision, using contrast and duration to prepare the visitor for a different mode of attention.
As visitors move along the corridor, real-time movements from the Nikkei 225 stock index are translated into synchronized visual and auditory patterns. Streams of light flow across a triptych of screens as individual stock fluctuations gather, separate, and form new alignments. Sound adds temporal depth to these movements, allowing the data to be perceived as a collective rhythm. This installation expresses emergence through the direct experience of micro-level events accumulating and interacting until a larger order becomes recognizable. SPARX’s investment philosophy is interwoven with the architecture, manifested through movement, sound, and varying intensities.
Digital art by siro, Silica, and backspacetokyo, combined with sound design by Oyster and lighting from ModuleX, function as parts of a cohesive spatial composition. The screens align with the path of travel; the darkness minimizes visual distractions, while the pale floor helps maintain orientation. A timber-lined opening interrupts the black corridor with a sudden burst of warmth, using material contrast to signal a change in program and pace. This interplay of white and black, silence and movement, smooth and textured surfaces creates a tactile language through which the company’s thinking is gradually revealed.
The journey continues into a gallery-like space designed as an evolving platform for SPARX’s social vision and future initiatives. This adaptable framework can accommodate changing content and new forms of presentation as the company evolves. Ideas are allowed to emerge through continuity, adaptation, and repeated encounters. The architecture avoids constraining the organization within a single corporate message; instead, it provides a setting in which its priorities can be revealed over time.


Adjacent lounges and meeting rooms shift the experience to a more intimate scale. Pale timber wraps the walls, ceilings, and integrated furnishings, while upholstered benches, shared tables, and acoustic surfaces facilitate waiting, conversation, reflection, and collaboration. The meeting room combines a formal conference table with a continuous bench and smaller tables along its edge, allowing for different patterns of use to coexist. In the communal lounge, a broad table faces a recessed refreshment counter, creating a social environment conducive to everyday activities such as making a drink, reading, exchanging ideas, or pausing between meetings. Controlled lighting and views of the city offer a calming atmosphere following the intensity of the data corridor.
These quieter rooms complete the project’s conceptual cycle. Small thoughts, informal exchanges, and individual observations are nurtured, allowing them to evolve into meaningful collective actions. Trust, focus, and openness are treated as vital components of the overall experience.

excerpt: Nora, NOMURA Co., Ltd. is transforming the supermarket experience with EARTH MART at Expo 2025 Osaka. This powerful exhibition focuses on food systems and sustainability, challenging our perceptions of daily dietary choices. The immersive spatial design leverages the familiar retail setting to reframe our understanding of life, consumption, and the future of food.
editorial:
EARTH MART opens with the language of an ordinary supermarket: aisles, display cases, packaged goods, and the familiar choreography of choosing what to eat. At Expo 2025 Osaka, this commercial framework becomes a public exhibition about life. Food is presented as a network of living systems, memories, labour, and decisions, offering visitors direct access to questions that might otherwise seem remote or abstract.
A central strength of the exhibition is its use of recognition. Visitors intuitively understand the supermarket setting, enabling the design to introduce moments of dislocation while maintaining clarity. Living vegetables emerge from dense planting beds, fish gather overhead as a suspended school, images of livestock accompany packaged meat, and rows of coloured ingredients fill refrigerator-like displays. Each scene is immediately legible, yet the familiar environment is subtly transformed to prompt a second look.
This approach gives physical form to the project’s concept of a "silent exhibition.” Information is conveyed through scale, repetition, scent, material, and juxtaposition, with explanatory text supporting the experience without overwhelming it. The pavilion prioritizes observation. A wall of ingredients translates abundance into colour and pattern. A monumental installation, created from the equivalent of 28,000 eggs (the average lifetime consumption in Japan, according to the submitted material), turns a commonplace food into an architectural measure of time.
The exhibition transitions between present-day food culture and speculative forms of eating. The submitted plan positions living vegetables, fish, and livestock at the start of the visitor journey, establishing food as a biological reality before the narrative broadens to include a future sushi restaurant, a kitchen capable of recording and recreating flavours, frozen and pulverized vegetables, experimental sweets, and an umeboshi project extending from 2025 to 2050. Technology enters through the established language of food, ensuring experimentation remains connected to appetite, craft, and daily experience.
Material choices reinforce this continuity between consumption and consequence. The submitted materials identify reused eggshells and living plant matter as exhibition elements, while contributions from farmers, sushi chefs, and biotechnology researchers extend the pavilion beyond a single authorial voice. Their expertise becomes part of the spatial narrative. The exhibition is presented as a constructed ecosystem of cultivation, preparation, preservation, consumption, and waste, with design serving as the structure that connects these various registers.
The plan is especially effective in treating circulation as a narrative sequence. Visitors move from displays of vegetables, fish, and livestock to sections focused on perception, measurement, technology, and shared food culture. “Receipts of the World,” “World’s Dining Table,” and the “Checkout Counter of Life” adopt the language of retail transactions, but their placement transforms the act of checking out into a moment for reflection. In the submitted drawing, the exit is described as the true entrance to EARTH MART: the world outside, where individual choices have consequences.
The final spaces temper the exhibition’s didactic potential through collective experience. A closing film centers on the image of a large shared table, with oversized projected foods creating a setting that is playful, social, and immediately understood across age groups. The pavilion concludes with conversation and appetite still present. Its argument is not that food should become a source of anxiety, but that careful attention can restore value to what convenience has made it easy to overlook.
EARTH MART remains grounded in everyday life. Its supermarket references provide clarity, while shifts in scale, material, lighting, and sequencing create enough distance for familiar objects to acquire new meaning. The pavilion renders food culture spatial, a field in which pleasure, responsibility, science, memory, and survival coexist.
